```{python}
import json
from pathlib import Path

import plotly.express as px
import polars as pl
from great_tables import GT
from IPython.display import display

metrics = {
    name: json.loads((Path(name) / "metrics.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    for name in ("jev", "gpt", "hybrid")
}
names = {
    "jev": "Jev 1.13.0",
    "gpt": "GPT-6 Luna",
    "hybrid": "Jev 1.13.0 → GPT-6 Luna",
}


def show(frame, formats=()):
    table = GT(frame)
    for columns, decimals in formats:
        table = table.fmt_number(columns=list(columns), decimals=decimals)
    display(table)


comparison = pl.DataFrame([
    {
        "Model or policy": names[name],
        "Accuracy": value["accuracy"],
        "Macro F1": value["macro_f1"],
        "P50 latency (ms)": value["latency_p50_ms"],
        "P95 latency (ms)": value["latency_p95_ms"],
        "Estimated USD / 1,000": value["cost_usd_per_1000"],
    }
    for name, value in metrics.items()
])
```

## Executive summary

This experiment evaluated whether a fast first-stage classifier could reduce
latency and cost while preserving the classification quality of an LLM-only
baseline across six languages.

The tested policy sends each message to **Jev 1.13.0** and accepts the result
when its maximum class probability is at least **0.72**. Lower-confidence or
invalid results fall back to **GPT-6 Luna**.

On a held-out 600-record multilingual test set, the hybrid achieved **0.973
macro F1**, compared with **0.968** for GPT-6 Luna alone. It reduced median
latency by approximately **74%**, reduced estimated cost per 1,000
classifications by approximately **22%**, and used GPT fallback for **7%** of
records. All predefined overall and language-level quality guardrails were met.

**Conclusion:** the results support the selective-routing approach and justify
advancing it to evaluation on representative real customer feedback. They do
not, by themselves, establish production performance because the benchmark data
are synthetic.

## Research question and decision criteria

The primary question was:

> Can Jev-first selective routing retain GPT-6 Luna-level sentiment quality
> while materially reducing response latency and cost?

The policy was evaluated against criteria defined before the held-out test was
run.

```{python}
criteria = pl.DataFrame([
    {
        "Criterion": "Overall macro F1",
        "Target": "Within 1 percentage point of GPT-6 Luna",
        "Observed": "+0.50 points; paired 95% CI −0.17 to +1.30",
        "Result": "Met",
    },
    {
        "Criterion": "Median latency",
        "Target": "At least 30% lower",
        "Observed": "Approximately 74% lower",
        "Result": "Met",
    },
    {
        "Criterion": "P95 latency",
        "Target": "No worse than GPT-6 Luna",
        "Observed": "Approximately 20% lower",
        "Result": "Met",
    },
    {
        "Criterion": "Estimated cost",
        "Target": "Below GPT-6 Luna",
        "Observed": "Approximately 22% lower per 1,000",
        "Result": "Met",
    },
    {
        "Criterion": "Language-level macro F1",
        "Target": "No language more than 3 points below baseline",
        "Observed": "Largest decrease: 0.99 points",
        "Result": "Met",
    },
])
show(criteria)
```

## Experiment design

Threshold selection and final evaluation were separated to reduce optimistic
bias. The routing threshold was chosen using a 600-record validation set and
then frozen at 0.72. The final policy was evaluated once on a separate,
previously untouched 600-record test set containing 100 records in each of
German, English, Spanish, French, Italian, and Portuguese. Each sentiment class
had 200 test records.

All strategies were evaluated on the same records. Quality differences were
therefore assessed with paired comparisons. Uncertainty for the overall
macro-F1 difference was estimated using 5,000 record-level bootstrap resamples.
The analysis emphasized effect sizes and predefined practical margins rather
than null-hypothesis significance testing.

## Overall results

```{python}
show(
    comparison,
    formats=(
        (("Accuracy", "Macro F1"), 3),
        (("P50 latency (ms)", "P95 latency (ms)"), 1),
        (("Estimated USD / 1,000",), 5),
    ),
)
```

The hybrid correctly classified 97.3% of test records and produced no
unresolved predictions. Its macro-F1 advantage over GPT-6 Luna was 0.50
percentage points. The paired 95% bootstrap interval ranged from −0.17 to +1.30
points, remaining well inside the predefined one-point maximum degradation.

The hybrid accepted 558 Jev results and routed 42 records to GPT-6 Luna. One
invalid Jev output was recollected once under the predefined collection policy;
the fresh response was valid. There were no unknown-cost attempts.

```{python}
latency = comparison.select(
    "Model or policy", "P50 latency (ms)", "P95 latency (ms)"
).unpivot(
    index="Model or policy", variable_name="Percentile", value_name="Latency (ms)"
)
px.bar(
    latency,
    x="Model or policy",
    y="Latency (ms)",
    color="Percentile",
    barmode="group",
    title="End-to-end latency comparison",
).show(renderer="notebook")
```

Median hybrid latency was 231 ms, compared with 885 ms for GPT-6 Luna. Hybrid
P95 was 1,073 ms, compared with 1,333 ms. The paired bootstrap intervals for
the hybrid-minus-GPT difference were −666 to −640 ms at P50 and −726 to −187
ms at P95.

The final-test hybrid latency is derived from fresh matched Jev timings plus the
fresh GPT stage time on routed fallbacks. An earlier controlled sequential pilot
directly timed the hybrid and supported the same operational conclusion.

## Performance by language

```{python}
languages = pl.DataFrame([
    {
        "Language": language.upper(),
        "Hybrid macro F1": values["macro_f1"],
        "GPT-6 Luna macro F1": metrics["gpt"]["by_language"][language]["macro_f1"],
        "Difference": values["macro_f1"] - metrics["gpt"]["by_language"][language]["macro_f1"],
    }
    for language, values in metrics["hybrid"]["by_language"].items()
])
show(
    languages,
    formats=((
        ("Hybrid macro F1", "GPT-6 Luna macro F1", "Difference"), 3
    ),),
)
```

Quality was equal to or higher than GPT-6 Luna in German, English, Spanish,
French, and Portuguese. Italian macro F1 was 0.99 percentage points lower,
remaining within the predefined three-point language guardrail. Each language
result is based on 100 records and should be interpreted as a guardrail rather
than a precise production estimate.

## Cost and operational implications

Estimated policy cost was **$0.01778 per 1,000 classifications**, compared with
**$0.02273** for GPT-6 Luna alone. These values are model-usage estimates, not
invoices, and may change with pricing or traffic mix.

The 7% fallback rate is the main source of the result: most messages receive the
faster Jev-only path, while GPT-6 Luna is reserved for lower-confidence cases.
Fallback requests necessarily incur both stages, which explains why hybrid tail
latency remains much higher than its median.

## Interpretation

The experiment provides consistent evidence that selective routing can preserve
sentiment-classification quality while improving typical response time and cost.
The conclusion is supported by:

- a threshold selected before the held-out evaluation;
- paired comparisons on identical records;
- an uncertainty interval tied to a practical quality margin;
- consistent overall, latency, cost, and language-level results; and
- complete coverage with no unresolved classifications.

Additional significance tests would add little to this decision. The main
remaining uncertainty is external validity—not sampling precision within this
synthetic benchmark.

## Limitations and recommended next step

The dataset is synthetic and may not reproduce real customer language,
misspellings, mixed sentiment, topic distribution, channel effects, message
length, class imbalance, or changes over time. The language slices are also too
small for detailed subgroup claims. P99 latency and concurrent-load behavior
were outside the scope of this experiment.

The recommended next investment is a privacy-reviewed and human-labeled sample
of real customer feedback reflecting the intended deployment environment. The
frozen 0.72 policy should be evaluated without retuning, with particular
attention to domain-specific errors, language coverage, fallback rate, latency,
and cost. This would test whether the observed benefit generalizes to production
traffic.

## Final conclusion

For this multilingual benchmark, **Jev 1.13.0 with GPT-6 Luna fallback below a
0.72 maximum-probability threshold met every predefined acceptance criterion**.
The policy matched or exceeded the LLM-only baseline in overall quality while
reducing median latency and estimated cost. The evidence supports moving from
synthetic benchmarking to a real-world validation study.
